n1: Ahmes is a robot classmate who is sure he's great at maths. He isn't. A child has to teach him.
n2: Better. But he trips when the tenths are tied. So the child spells out the whole rule, place by place.
c2: If the tenths are the same, check the next place, and if every place is the same, they're equal.
n3: Forty out of forty. Notice the panel: the child's own words, each tied to the line of code it became. A language model on Vultr Serverless Inference compiles them literally. Say it vaguely, and he gets partly wrong code. Then plain arithmetic grades him. Never AI.
n4: Now fractions. Some explanations are dangerous.
c3: Keep doubling both bottoms until they're the same.
n5: That loop never ends. The container on a Vultr server was killed at three seconds, and destroyed. The app never noticed.
n6: Try to break him. Copy your notes twice, again and again: out of memory, killed at sixty-four megabytes. Beyond the guard, call the internet: network is unreachable. And afterwards, the sandbox log says no containers are running.
n7: Under the hood: the browser talks to Caddy, then a FastAPI app on Vultr Cloud Compute in Madrid, which starts one container per task. Every language model call goes to Vultr Serverless Inference, running qwen three point eight, twenty-seven b. Ahmes's voice is ElevenLabs, reading only his own lines. A sweeper removes strays, and every removal is verified.
n8: In 1978, computers diagnosed children's maths bugs. Now children debug the computer.
n9: Teach Ahmes. A prototype, built on Vultr for Agent Rush.
